title: Before Elevating Leaders, Give Them an Inside View of Different Experiences
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This short Admired Leadership post argues that new jobs, challenges and experiences develop leaders faster and better than classroom training. It cites decades of research showing that leaders credit stretch assignments on the job for shaping them. In large organizations the author says job rotation across functions, businesses and geographies outperforms every other development investment and can predict who gets promoted. In smaller enterprises, where formal rotation is hard, the equivalent is giving people accountability for something new such as a new market, a new client or an unsolved problem. The worked example is Dana McNabb, soon to be General Mills' first woman CEO, whose 27 years moved her through cereal, snacks, dairy, Europe, strategy, retail and pet food. The conclusion is a practical rule for any organization: sample many experiences before promoting someone to bigger responsibility.
points: Leaders learn most from assignments that stretch them on the job, so experience is the primary development tool and training a distant second.

In large organizations job rotation beats every other development investment and even predicts promotion, while smaller firms can substitute accountability for a new market, client or unsolved problem.

Dana McNabb's path across marketing, strategy, international operations and retail illustrates how moving through many parts of a company gives a future CEO an inside view and a web of relationships no single track could.
The actionable rule is to give future leaders a range of assignments before elevating them, so they arrive already knowing the organization.
quotes: Decades of research on how leaders grow point to the fact that leaders learn most from assignments that stretch them, not from the classroom.

In larger organizations, job rotation outperforms every other development investment. Moving talented people across functions, businesses, and geographies broadens their knowledge, accelerates their skill development, and can predict who gets promoted.

In smaller enterprises, where formal rotation is harder to arrange, the game changer is giving people accountability for something new, such as a new market, a new client, or a problem no one has solved.
Having moved through so many parts of the organization, she learned from the inside what no single career track could teach her.

Before elevating the best people, give them an inside view of many experiences. By the time they take on bigger responsibility, they will already know the organization and possess a diverse set of skills to make an impact.
Every new assignment gives leaders a lesson no promotion or training program can provide.
